rows.stem: Which by-product is obtained in the manufacture of phenol from cumene ?
rows.solution:
The by-product is ACETONE.

In the cumene process, cumene is oxidised by air to cumene hydroperoxide, and treating that with dilute acid cleaves it into two fragments — phenol and acetone:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH(CH_3)_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{O_2}} \mathrm{C_6H_5C(CH_3)_2OOH} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H_2O}]{\mathrm{H^+}} \mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + \mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}\)

The economics of the route rest on that by-product: both halves of the cumene molecule end up as something worth selling, which is why this is the industrial method.

rows.stem: Which reagents are required for one step conversion of chlorobenzene to toluene ?
rows.solution:
The reagents are METHYL CHLORIDE, SODIUM AND DRY ETHER — the Wurtz-Fittig reaction.

Sodium in dry ether couples an ARYL halide with an ALKYL halide, joining the two carbon skeletons directly, so chlorobenzene and methyl chloride give toluene in one step:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5Cl} + \mathrm{CH_3Cl} + 2\mathrm{Na} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CH_3} + 2\mathrm{NaCl}\)

The Friedel-Crafts option is the trap. Methyl chloride with anhydrous aluminium chloride would methylate a benzene ring, but it cannot be used here — the chlorine is already on the ring, and the product would be a chlorotoluene, not toluene.

rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem: Coordination number of Fe in \(\mathrm{[Fe(C_2O_4)_3]^{3-}}\) is :
rows.solution:
The coordination number is SIX.

Coordination number counts DONOR ATOMS attached to the metal, not ligand molecules. The oxalate ion is BIDENTATE: it binds through two of its oxygen atoms at once, closing a five-membered chelate ring.

Three oxalate ligands therefore supply \(3 \times 2 = 6\) donor atoms, and the complex is octahedral.

Counting the three ligands instead of the six donor atoms gives 3, which is the answer the question is testing for.

rows.stem: Which of the following complexes shows geometrical isomerism ?
rows.solution:
The complex that shows geometrical isomerism is \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4Cl_2]^{+}}\).

Geometrical isomerism needs at least TWO KINDS of ligand distributed so that their arrangement can differ. In an octahedral complex of the type \(\mathrm{MA_4B_2}\) the two chlorido ligands may sit next to one another, giving the CIS isomer, or opposite one another, giving the TRANS isomer.

The other three cannot. \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\) has only one kind of ligand; \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5Cl]^{2+}}\) has a single chlorido ligand, and one ligand has no second one to be cis or trans to; \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5(ONO)]^{2+}}\) shows LINKAGE isomerism instead, the nitrite ion being able to bind through nitrogen or through oxygen.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: Which of the following does **not** show variable oxidation state ?
rows.solution:
SCANDIUM does not show variable oxidation states.

Scandium is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^1 4s^2\). Losing all three of those electrons gives \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\), which has the argon configuration — an empty \(3d\) subshell and nothing further to give or gain. Scandium has no other stable state, and its \(+3\) compounds are white and diamagnetic, unlike the coloured paramagnetic compounds of the rest of the series.

Manganese runs from \(+2\) to \(+7\), chromium from \(+2\) to \(+6\), and copper shows \(+1\) and \(+2\), so all three of those are variable.

rows.stem: The reagent that can be used to convert benzenediazonium chloride to benzene is :
rows.solution:
The reagent is ETHANOL, \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH}\).

Ethanol reduces the diazonium group, replacing it by hydrogen and being itself oxidised to ethanal, so the nitrogen leaves as a gas and the bare ring is left behind:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-} + \mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_6} + \mathrm{N_2} + \mathrm{CH_3CHO} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

Water gives phenol instead, and copper(I) cyanide gives benzonitrile — both replace the diazonium group with something rather than with hydrogen. Hypophosphorous acid would serve in place of ethanol, but it is not among the options.

rows.stem: The gas evolved when methylamine reacts with \(\mathrm{HNO_2}\) is :
rows.solution:
The gas evolved is NITROGEN, \(\mathrm{N_2}\).

Methylamine is a primary ALIPHATIC amine, and the diazonium salt such an amine forms with nitrous acid is unstable even in the cold. It breaks up at once, nitrogen escaping as a gas and the carbocation left behind picking up water:
\(\mathrm{CH_3NH_2} + \mathrm{HNO_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3OH} + \mathrm{N_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The brisk effervescence of nitrogen is in fact the standard test for a primary aliphatic amine. Aniline is the contrast: its diazonium salt is stabilised by the ring and survives at 273-278 K, so no nitrogen comes off until it is warmed.

rows.stem: A solution of acetone in chloroform :

options.label: C
options.text: shows a positive deviation from Raoult’s law.

options.label: D
options.text: shows a negative deviation from Raoult’s law.

rows.solution:
A solution of acetone in chloroform shows a NEGATIVE DEVIATION from Raoult's law.

Neither liquid hydrogen bonds to itself: acetone has no hydrogen on an electronegative atom, and the hydrogen of chloroform is held by carbon. Put them together and a NEW hydrogen bond becomes possible — the chloroform hydrogen, made acidic by the three chlorines pulling on it, bonds to the lone pair on the acetone oxygen.

The interaction between UNLIKE molecules is therefore STRONGER than that between like molecules. The molecules escape less readily than Raoult's law predicts, the observed vapour pressure is lower, mixing is exothermic and the volume contracts slightly.

rows.stem: A galvanic cell can behave like an electrolytic cell when
rows.solution:
A galvanic cell behaves like an electrolytic cell when \(\mathrm{E_{ext} > E_{cell}}\).

Left alone, a galvanic cell drives its own reaction and pushes electrons out. Apply an opposing external voltage and three things can happen. While the external voltage is SMALLER than the cell's own, the cell still wins and the reaction continues in its spontaneous direction. When the two are EQUAL the current stops altogether and the cell is at equilibrium — which is how a cell's potential is measured without drawing current from it.

Once the external voltage EXCEEDS the cell's, it overpowers it: current is forced through in the opposite direction, the electrode reactions reverse, and electrical energy is now being spent to drive a non-spontaneous chemical change. That is exactly what an electrolytic cell does — and it is also how a lead storage battery is recharged.

rows.stem: The value of rate constant for a pseudo first order reaction :

options.label: B
options.text: depends on the concentration of reactants present in small amount.

options.label: C
options.text: depends on the concentration of reactants present in large excess.

options.label: D
options.text: is not dependent on the concentration of reactants.

rows.solution:
The rate constant of a pseudo first order reaction DEPENDS ON THE CONCENTRATION OF THE REACTANT PRESENT IN LARGE EXCESS.

A pseudo first order reaction is really a second order one in disguise. The hydrolysis of an ester, for instance, involves both the ester and water, so
\(\text{Rate} = k[\text{ester}][\mathrm{H_2O}]\)

Water is also the solvent and is present in enormous excess, so its concentration barely changes and can be treated as a constant. Absorbing it into the constant gives
\(\text{Rate} = k'[\text{ester}]\) with \(k' = k[\mathrm{H_2O}]\)

The observed constant \(k'\) therefore carries that concentration inside it, and would take a different value in a different excess. A genuine first order constant depends on temperature alone; this one does not, which is what the prefix "pseudo" is warning about.

rows.stem: Furanose ring of fructose is formed due to reaction between :
rows.solution:
The furanose ring of fructose is formed between \(\mathrm{C_2}\) AND \(\mathrm{C_5}\).

Fructose is a KETOhexose — its carbonyl group is at \(\mathrm{C_2}\), not at \(\mathrm{C_1}\) as in glucose. The ring therefore closes onto \(\mathrm{C_2}\), and the hydroxyl group that reaches it is the one on \(\mathrm{C_5}\), giving a cyclic hemiketal.

Count the members: \(\mathrm{C_2}\), \(\mathrm{C_3}\), \(\mathrm{C_4}\), \(\mathrm{C_5}\) and the bridging oxygen — a FIVE membered ring, which is why it is named after furan.

The contrast with glucose is the point. Glucose closes \(\mathrm{C_1}\) to \(\mathrm{C_5}\) and gets a six membered pyranose ring; fructose starts one carbon further along and gets a five membered one from the same span of the chain.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Actinoids show wide range of oxidation states.
Reason (R) : This is due to comparable energies of 5f, 6d and 7s orbitals.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Actinoids do show a wide range of oxidation states — uranium runs from \(+3\) to \(+6\), and neptunium and plutonium reach \(+7\).

And the cause is exactly what the Reason gives. In the actinoids the \(5f\), \(6d\) and \(7s\) orbitals lie so close together in energy that electrons from all three sets are available for bonding, and there is no strong preference for stopping at any one number. The lanthanoids are the contrast: there the \(4f\) orbitals are buried well below the valence level, so nearly all lanthanoids are restricted to \(+3\).

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Order of the reaction can be zero or fractional.
Reason (R) : We cannot determine order from balanced chemical equation.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true, but the Reason is NOT the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Order can indeed be zero or fractional — a zero order reaction is one whose rate does not depend on concentration at all, as in a surface-catalysed decomposition, and fractional orders arise from complex multi-step mechanisms.

And it is true that order cannot be read off a balanced equation; it has to be measured.

But the second does not EXPLAIN the first. What makes zero and fractional orders possible is that order is a property of the MECHANISM, in particular of the slowest step, rather than of the stoichiometry. The Reason states a consequence of that same fact — it runs alongside the Assertion rather than accounting for it.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Boiling point of \(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_2NH}\) is lower than that of \(n\text{-}\mathrm{C_4H_9NH_2}\).
Reason (R) : Hydrogen bonding is much more extensive in \(n\text{-}\mathrm{C_4H_9NH_2}\) as compared to \(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_2NH}\).
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

The two compounds have the same molecular formula and nearly the same mass, so the difference must come from hydrogen bonding, and that depends on how many hydrogens sit on the nitrogen.

Butan-1-amine is a PRIMARY amine with TWO hydrogens on nitrogen, so its molecules associate strongly with one another. Diethylamine is SECONDARY and has only ONE, so it associates less. Fewer hydrogen bonds mean less energy needed to separate the molecules, so diethylamine boils LOWER, at about 329 K against about 351 K.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Phenol is less acidic than alcohol.
Reason (R) : Phenoxide ion is more stable than alkoxide ion.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is FALSE while the Reason is TRUE.

Phenol is the STRONGER acid, not the weaker — \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) about 10 against about 16 for an alcohol.

The Reason is correct as stated, and it is precisely why the Assertion fails. In the phenoxide ion the negative charge is delocalised into the benzene ring by resonance, spread over the ortho and para carbons as well as the oxygen. The alkoxide ion has no such escape: its charge sits entirely on one oxygen, and the alkyl group pushes still more density onto it.

The more stable the anion, the more readily the parent gives up its proton — so a more stable phenoxide means a MORE acidic phenol, the opposite of what the Assertion claims.

rows.stem: State Raoult’s law for a solution containing volatile components. Why is the vapour pressure of an aqueous solution of glucose lower than that of water ?
rows.solution:
RAOULT'S LAW for a solution of volatile components. For a solution of two or more volatile liquids, the partial vapour pressure of each component is directly proportional to its MOLE FRACTION in the solution:
\(p_1 = p_1^{\,\circ}\,x_1\) and \(p_2 = p_2^{\,\circ}\,x_2\)
where \(p_1^{\,\circ}\) and \(p_2^{\,\circ}\) are the vapour pressures of the pure components, and the total vapour pressure is \(p = p_1 + p_2\).

Why an aqueous GLUCOSE solution has the lower vapour pressure. Glucose is a NON-VOLATILE solute, so it contributes nothing to the vapour above the solution; the whole vapour pressure comes from the water. Its molecules do, however, occupy part of the surface, so fewer water molecules are present at the surface and the escaping tendency of the water is reduced.

Put quantitatively, the mole fraction of water is now less than 1, so by Raoult's law \(p = p^{\,\circ}x_{\text{water}}\) is less than \(p^{\,\circ}\). The lowering depends on how many solute particles there are and not on what they are, which is what makes it a colligative property.

rows.stem:
Draw the structures of the major monohalo products in each of the following reactions :

(a) 4-(Hydroxymethyl)phenol \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{SOCl_2}}\) ?

(b) 3-Phenylprop-1-ene + HBr \(\xrightarrow{\text{peroxide}}\) ?
rows.solution:
(a) 4-(Hydroxymethyl)phenol carries TWO hydroxyl groups — one alcoholic, on the \(-\mathrm{CH_2OH}\) side chain, and one phenolic, on the ring. Thionyl chloride attacks only the ALCOHOLIC one. The phenolic hydroxyl is unreactive towards it, because its \(\mathrm{C-OH}\) bond has partial double bond character from resonance with the ring and will not break.

So the chlorine replaces the side-chain hydroxyl and the ring hydroxyl is left alone:

Product: 4-(chloromethyl)phenol, \(\mathrm{HO{-}C_6H_4{-}CH_2Cl}\) with the two groups para to each other.

(b) 3-Phenylprop-1-ene is \(\mathrm{C_6H_5{-}CH_2{-}CH{=}CH_2}\), and the PEROXIDE changes the mechanism. Without it the addition would be ionic and Markovnikov, putting the bromine on the middle carbon. With it the addition is by free radicals, and the rule reverses — this is the anti-Markovnikov, or peroxide, effect.

The bromine radical adds to the TERMINAL carbon, because the radical left on the middle carbon is secondary and therefore the more stable of the two:

Product: 1-bromo-3-phenylpropane, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5{-}CH_2{-}CH_2{-}CH_2{-}Br}\).

Note that the peroxide effect works only with hydrogen bromide, not with the other halogen acids — which is why the question specifies it.

rows.stem:
How can you obtain the following from aniline ? Give only chemical equation.

(a) \(p\)-nitroaniline

(b) Chlorobenzene

(c) Phenol
rows.solution:
(a) p-NITROANILINE. Nitrating aniline directly fails: the nitrating mixture is strongly acidic, it protonates the amino group, and the resulting anilinium ion is meta directing, so a large amount of the meta isomer appears. The amino group must therefore be PROTECTED first by acetylation, nitrated as the amide, and then freed again by hydrolysis:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} \xrightarrow[\text{pyridine}]{(\mathrm{CH_3CO})_2\mathrm{O}} \mathrm{C_6H_5NHCOCH_3} \xrightarrow[288\ \mathrm{K}]{\mathrm{HNO_3}/\mathrm{H_2SO_4}} \mathrm{p\text{-}O_2N{-}C_6H_4{-}NHCOCH_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H^+}\ \text{or}\ \mathrm{OH^-}} \mathrm{p\text{-}O_2N{-}C_6H_4{-}NH_2}\)

(b) CHLOROBENZENE, by diazotisation followed by the Sandmeyer reaction. The diazonium group is replaced by chloride in the presence of copper(I) chloride:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} \xrightarrow[273\text{-}278\ \mathrm{K}]{\mathrm{NaNO_2}/\mathrm{HCl}} \mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{HCl}]{\mathrm{Cu_2Cl_2}} \mathrm{C_6H_5Cl} + \mathrm{N_2}\)

(c) PHENOL, from the same diazonium salt simply by warming it with water:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} \xrightarrow[273\text{-}278\ \mathrm{K}]{\mathrm{NaNO_2}/\mathrm{HCl}} \mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-} \xrightarrow[\text{warm}]{\mathrm{H_2O}} \mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + \mathrm{N_2} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

All three routes turn on the same fact: the diazonium group is an excellent leaving group, which makes it the standard way of putting onto a benzene ring a substituent that cannot be introduced directly.
